questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities and hearing good things about the city and the study environment.

Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Easy. UT Law is very good at communicating.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is very difficult to find reasonably priced and decent housing in Austin for the Fall semester only. Staying at a co-op (College Houses or ICC) is an easy way to find housing, because the co-ops are established non-profits and you can rent for the Fall semester only. Staying at a co-op is a relatively cheap option, but the co-ops are really worn-down, and some of them are infamous for loud parties several times during the week, drugs, rats and cockroaches. I stayed at Halstead and it was one of the better co-ops, but it was still very dirty. However, I felt like it was a good trade-off compared to paying a lot more for the for-profit student housing off campus. In the Spring I would also recommend looking in Facebook group for subleases/ lease takeovers.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Most undergrad students and exchange students live in West Campus which felt relatively safe. Some law students live closer to the Law School which also felt safe and a little more "grown up". Generally, I think living off campus was nice, but be mindful of the area because some parts of Austin are not safe at night.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Unless you are very lucky it is going to be a trade-off between spending a lot of money on housing or living in something that is old and dirty. However, most places where students live are very social, so it will be fun no matter what.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The international office at UT Law helps exchange students register, so it was very easy!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You register during the first week in an online system. There is an add/ drop period where you can change your courses in the same system. Don't worry about the process at all - UT Law will guide you through it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Lots of help form the international office at UT Law. They guide you through the process and answer any questions you have.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got most of the classes I wanted (4 out of 5) but I dropped one of my classes and had trouble finding a replacement during the add/ drop period.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry about it, and use the add/ drop period if you change your mind.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Challenging courses, but the workload was mostly appropriate.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At UT Law they use the socratic method in many courses where they cold-call students. Generally, you are expected to be well prepared for class and to participate.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
U.S. Constitutional Law for Foreign Lawyers
Antitrust
Wall Street Regulation
Corporations and the Constitution
Directed Research and Study

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Wall Street Regulation was a fun class and the workload was very light. The professor specifically tries to make it a low stress class. I also really enjoyed Corporations and the Constitution which is a seminar class with Prof. Sepper who is a very good teacher. However, I would only recommend taking seminar classes if you are actually interested in the topic because it's pretty time consuming to write a seminar paper.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you live at a co-op, food is included in the rent, but I bought some additional groceries because depending on the co-op there won't be ingredients for personal cooking etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books cost about 3000 kr. for the semester even though I bought as much as possible used which was more than I expected. Insurance is very expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds! There are a lot of opportunities if you look for them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn't really use the clubs, but there are free gyms on campus. Greg Gym has a great recreational pool, and it is free to use it as a student. I would also recommend going to as many sports events as possible. Football is a big event and you should experience it at least once. Basketball is also fun, and the women's volleyball team is really good.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go on trips, both in Texas and in other states. We went hiking in Big Bend National Park in Texas, visited Houston, New Orleans, Chicago etc. Domestic flights are expensive, but you can really get a lot out of a weekend/ holiday.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it's very easy to adjust to the U.S., but Texas can be a pretty special state in some way.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to the people you live with and have classes with! People are very friendly and are happy to show you fun things to do in Austin.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Texas is built for driving, and the locals pretty much drive to everything. That can be challenging if you don't have a car but want to join an event, but people are happy to give you a ride if you ask.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness! Texans are generally very good at talking with strangers.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Keep an open mind
2. Travel as much a possible
3. Go dancing on a traditional Texas dance bar! (White Horse was our favorite!)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The busses are free for UT students. They are unreliable, but they can take you most places on campus and downtown when it is too hot to walk (which it pretty much is from August to November...)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Travelling and meeting new people from around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Accepting the poor housing conditions.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
